# Why Brake Work Can Trigger AWD Alerts on a Ford Edge

When a mechanic or family member performs brake maintenance, it is easy to overlook the electrical implications of removing wheels. In your specific case regarding the 2016 Ford Edge, the sequence of symptomsâa chemical smell followed by intermittent "AWD Temporarily Disabled" warningsâpoints directly to a wiring issue rather than an anti-seize application error.

The most probable culprit is the ABS wheel speed sensor ring (tone ring) or the sensor itself located near the brake rotor. These components are critical for the Electronic Stability Control (ESC) and Anti-lock Braking System (ABS), which are inextricably linked to the All-Wheel Drive system in Ford vehicles of this generation. If the AWD module cannot receive accurate wheel speed data from even one wheel, it logically defaults to a two-wheel-drive mode to prevent drivetrain binding or loss of control.

When rotors are removed, there is a high risk of damaging the delicate toothed ring etched onto the rotor's inner hub or knocking off debris that covers it. The "chemical" smell you detected is almost certainly burning electrical insulation or overheated wiring. This suggests that a wire pinched between the caliper and the suspension bracket was compromised during reassembly, or that a connector was not fully seated, creating an intermittent short to ground as the suspension moves over bumps.

### Diagnosing the Sensor Circuit

To verify this hypothesis without immediately disassembling the brakes again, you can use an OBD-II scanner capable of reading manufacturer-specific codes. While generic scanners might only show "P0562 System Voltage Low," Ford-specific diagnostics will reveal codes like **C1A43** (Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor Circuit) or **C1A83** (Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor Circuit).

If the code indicates an open circuit or high resistance, check the connector behind the caliper. On many 2016 Edges, the ABS sensor plug is tucked into a tight space near the steering knuckle. If the anti-seize compound was applied to the threads of the lug nuts but accidentally smeared onto the electrical contacts within the wheel well, it could cause erratic readings. However, anti-seize on metal threads is safe; it only becomes problematic if it migrates to sensitive electronic components or seals.

### The Role of Anti-Seize and Debris

Anti-seize lubricant is essential for preventing seized lug nuts, particularly on vehicles with carbon-based wheel bearings or in salt-heavy climates. However, the application technique matters. If the old rotors were stuck due to rust or paint rather than seized bearings, using excessive force during removal can warp the hub face or knock off the tone ring teeth.

Once the new rotor is bolted down, ensure no debris from the old caliper bracket or suspension components has fallen onto the tone ring. The sensor reads the magnetic field changes created by these teeth spinning past it. If a piece of metal shavings bridges the gap between the sensor and the ring, or if the ring itself is physically damaged, the signal will be interrupted.

### Clearing the Warning Light

If the wiring check reveals no shorts and the tone rings are intact, the issue may be a transient fault that cleared itself after the vehicle cooled down. However, if the "AWD Temporarily Disabled" message returns, the system has detected a persistent fault. You will need to address the electrical connection before driving the vehicle further.

Driving with an intermittent wheel speed sensor failure is dangerous. The stability control system relies on comparing left and right wheel speeds to detect skidding. If one side reports false data, the ESC may engage braking unexpectedly or fail to intervene during emergency maneuvers. Since the AWD system defaults to a safe mode when faults are detected, you can likely drive cautiously in two-wheel-drive mode until repairs are made, but do not rely on AWD capabilities until the sensor circuit is confirmed functional.
